sessions.title: A direction the map does not turn away
sessions.focus: Define eigenvectors/eigenvalues from invariant one-dimensional directions, distinguish direction preservation from fixed vectors or preserved length, and derive repeated action along one eigenvector.
sessions.purpose: M14 taught what a linear map does to arbitrary vectors. M16 begins by asking whether any nonzero directions are special enough that the map only rescales them; the concept must exist before the characteristic-polynomial recipe.
sessions.centralCapability: Given a finite real linear map and fresh candidate vectors, verify or refute eigenvector status from Av=λv, interpret the invariant line, and use λ to predict repeated action along that direction.
sessions.principalObstacle: A learner may confuse Av=v with Av=λv, preserved norm with preserved direction, or allow v=0 because A0=λ0 for every λ.
entryPrerequisites: M13 nonzero vectors, scalar multiples and span(v)
M14 matrix-vector action and finite linear maps
M02/M09 scalar powers for repeated action
requiredOwnership: Verify eigenpair status Av=λv for supplied nonzero real candidates by exact proportionality, recovering λ when it exists.
Use linearity to justify that a nonzero scalar rescaling of a verified eigenvector represents the same eigendirection and retains the same eigenvalue.

sessions.applicationScope: Exact finite real 2D/3D linear maps; candidate directions are checked directly without characteristic polynomials.
sessions.transferScope: Audit an orthogonal rotation that preserves length but has no nonzero real eigenvector, forcing the learner to reject preserved-length reasoning.
inScope: repeated action on a verified eigenvector
sessions.exitCondition: On a fresh linear map, verify/refute candidate eigenvectors, identify λ when it exists, explain the invariant line and use the verified eigenpair to predict repeated action without matrix-power brute force.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. M14 taught us to apply a linear map to any vector. Now ask a more structural question: is there a nonzero direction that the map does not turn away from itself? If A sends a nonzero vector v to a scalar multiple of itself, Av=λv, then v is an eigenvector and λ is its eigenvalue. The line span(v) is invariant because every point cv on that line is sent to A(cv)=cAv=cλv, which is still on the same line.

Definition discipline. The vector must be nonzero. If v=0 were admitted, A0=λ0 would hold for every λ and the word eigenvalue would stop identifying anything. The scalar λ is allowed to be zero: for P=diag(1,0), e2=(0,1) is nonzero and Pe2=0=0e2. A negative λ reverses orientation along the same line; |λ|>1 stretches and |λ|<1 shrinks. Only λ=1 makes every eigenvector on that line a fixed vector.

Worked example. Let A=[[2,1],[0,1]]. For e1=(1,0), Ae1=(2,0)=2e1, so e1 is an eigenvector with λ=2. For w=(1,-1), Aw=(1,-1)=w, so w is an eigenvector with λ=1. But e2=(0,1) maps to (1,1), which is not a scalar multiple of e2, so e2 is not an eigenvector. The decisive test is exact proportionality, not whether the image merely looks similar.

Connect. If Av=λv and c≠0, then A(cv)=cAv=cλv=λ(cv), so all nonzero vectors on the same invariant line share the same eigenvalue. This is about a direction/subspace, even though we represent it by particular nonzero vectors.

Repeated action. Once Av=λv, apply A again: A²v=A(λv)=λAv=λ²v. Induction gives A^k v=λ^k v for every integer k≥0. This conclusion is earned only after the eigenpair is verified.

Guided practice. Let C=[[3,0],[2,1]]. Test u=(1,1), v=(0,1), and r=(1,0). For every eigenvector, identify λ and the invariant line. Then predict C^4u without multiplying four matrices.

Fade. The fixed Main changes both the matrix and candidate directions; the Transfer changes the representation entirely to a rotation audit. No fixed answer is solved in the lesson.

Distinction check. Fixed vector means λ=1. Preserved length says ||Av||=||v||. Eigenvector says Av is exactly a real scalar multiple of the nonzero v. These are different properties.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. Cu=(3,3)=3u, so u has λ=3 and invariant line span(1,1). Cv=(0,1)=v, so v has λ=1 and invariant line span(0,1). Cr=(3,2) is not proportional to r, so r is not an eigenvector. Therefore C^4u=3^4u=81(1,1)=(81,81).

T22V3::SIDE279::S01-M@1.prompt: Let A=[[1,2],[2,1]]. Consider p=(1,1), q=(2,-2), and r=(1,0). (a) For each candidate, compute Av and decide whether it is an eigenvector over R; when it is, state λ. (b) Explain why q and (1,-1) represent the same eigendirection and must have the same eigenvalue; include the general linearity step A(cv)=λ(cv) for c≠0 once Av=λv. (c) Without multiplying A by itself five times, compute A^5 p and justify the shortcut from the verified eigenpair.

T22V3::SIDE279::S01-T@1.prompt: Let R=[[0,-1],[1,0]]. A report says: “R preserves the length of every vector, so every nonzero vector is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 1; in particular e1=(1,0) is fixed.” Audit the report. Give a decisive geometric or algebraic reason that the length claim does not imply the eigenvector claim, test e1 directly, and determine whether R has any nonzero real eigenvector.

T22V3::SIDE279::S01-M@1.reference: Ap=(3,3)=3p, so p is an eigenvector with λ=3. Aq=(-2,2)=-q, so q is an eigenvector with λ=-1. Ar=(1,2), not a scalar multiple of r, so r is not an eigenvector. Since q=2(1,-1), both nonzero vectors lie on the same invariant line; if Av=λv then A(cv)=λ(cv) for c≠0, so they share λ=-1. Finally A^5p=3^5p=243(1,1)=(243,243).

rubric.criterion: Computes all three images and correctly classifies p, q and r, including λ=3 and λ=-1 for the eigenvectors.
Uses linearity to show that nonzero scalar rescaling preserves the eigendirection and eigenvalue, and applies it correctly to q and (1,-1).
Uses the verified eigenpair Ap=3p to justify A^5p=3^5p=(243,243) without brute-force matrix powers.

T22V3::SIDE279::S01-M@1.marking: Score only public obligations. Accept any exact proportionality argument and any valid derivation of the repeated-action result.

T22V3::SIDE279::S01-T@1.reference: R is a 90-degree rotation, so it preserves Euclidean length but changes every nonzero real direction. Re1=(0,1)≠e1 and is not a scalar multiple of e1. Algebraically, if R(a,b)=λ(a,b) with real λ and (a,b)≠(0,0), then -b=λa and a=λb. Substitution gives (1+λ^2)a=0; if a=0 then b=0, contradiction, so λ^2=-1, impossible for real λ. Thus R has no nonzero real eigenvector. Preserved norm is not preserved direction.

rubric.criterion: Separates length preservation from eigenvector direction preservation and rejects the report's inference.
Tests e1 directly and shows Re1=(0,1) is not a scalar multiple of e1.
Correctly concludes there is no nonzero real eigenvector, with a decisive geometric rotation argument or equivalent real algebraic derivation.
